job.style: a market or shop situation that uses the idea

passage: Rohan runs a small stationery shop where he sells notebooks in bundles. He recently received a shipment of 4x^2 - 16 notebooks. To organize his shelf, he decides to factorise this expression. He knows that 4x^2 - 16 is a difference of two squares, which follows the identity a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b). By taking out the common factor of 4, he gets 4(x^2 - 4), which then simplifies to 4(x - 2)(x + 2). A customer asks for 3x + 9 notebooks, and Rohan explains that he can factorise this as 3(x + 3). He emphasizes that when he takes out the common factor 3, the term 3x becomes x and the 9 becomes 3, because 3 divided by 3 leaves 1. Later, he helps a student with the expression x^2 - 6x + 9. He warns the student that this is a perfect square trinomial, (x - 3)^2, not (x - 3)(x + 3). Finally, he shows that if he has 2x + 4, he can write it as 2(x + 2). He checks his work by multiplying 2 by x and 2 by 2 to get back to 2x + 4, ensuring his factorisation is correct. He reminds everyone that every number has at least two factors: 1 and itself.

items.evidence: By taking out the common factor of 4, he gets 4(x^2 - 4), which then simplifies to 4(x - 2)(x + 2).
items.q: Rohan starts with 4x^2 - 16. Which form shows it completely factorised?
items.explain: x^2 - 4 still splits into (x - 2)(x + 2), so the full answer is 4(x - 2)(x + 2).

wrong.why: thinks a bracket means it is fully factorised
thinks a^2 - b^2 is the same as (a - b)^2
uses 4 instead of its square root 2

items.evidence: He warns the student that this is a perfect square trinomial, (x - 3)^2, not (x - 3)(x + 3).
items.q: A student factorises x^2 - 6x + 9 as (x - 3)(x + 3). What should Rohan say?
options: It is (x - 3)^2, a perfect square
It is (x - 3)(x + 3), a difference of squares
It is (x + 3)^2, since 9 is positive
It is (x - 9)^2, using the last term
items.explain: Rohan says x^2 - 6x + 9 is a perfect square trinomial, (x - 3)^2, not (x - 3)(x + 3).

wrong.why: thinks any minus with squares gives (x - 3)(x + 3)
ignores the signs when finding the numbers
uses the constant 9 without taking its root

items.evidence: He checks his work by multiplying 2 by x and 2 by 2 to get back to 2x + 4, ensuring his factorisation is correct.
items.q: Meena factorises 5x + 10 as 5(x + 2). What would Rohan advise her to do next?
options: She should multiply back to get 5x + 10
She should skip checking, as steps are enough
She should take 5 out again from x + 2
She should check only that 5 divides 10
items.explain: Like Rohan with 2(x + 2), multiplying back to the original expression shows the factorisation is correct.

wrong.why: thinks following steps makes checking unnecessary
thinks factors can be taken out again and again
thinks only the number parts matter

items.evidence: He reminds everyone that every number has at least two factors: 1 and itself.
items.q: Priya says the only factor of 7 is 7. What has she missed?
options: 1 is also a factor of 7
0 is also a factor of 7
7 itself is not a factor of 7
14 is also a factor of 7
items.explain: Every number has at least two factors, 1 and itself, so 7 has factors 1 and 7.

wrong.why: thinks zero counts as a factor
thinks a number is not its own factor

items.evidence: He knows that 4x^2 - 16 is a difference of two squares, which follows the identity a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b).
items.q: Why can Rohan use the identity (a - b)(a + b) for 4x^2 - 16?
options: Its two terms are squares, one minus the other
It equals (2x - 4)^2, a perfect square
Any two squares fit, added or subtracted
Both of its terms have 4 as a factor
items.explain: The identity a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b) works because 4x^2 - 16 is a difference of two squares.

wrong.why: thinks a^2 - b^2 is the same as (a - b)^2
thinks a sum of squares also factorises this way
picks a true detail that is not the reason
